extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century literary criticism; poets, authors, and literary reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-evaluative criteria for assessing poets, prose writers, and dramatists (style, imagination, subject-suitability, originality, dramatic craft) as presented in a 19th‑century review essay. Emphasizes qualities like truth of representation, unity, taste, and stage-craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for serious subjects ('writes verses, not a poem')
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Moore ought not to contend with serious difficulties or with entire subjects. He can write verses, not a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assigning or attempting grand, continuous themes if the author lacks principle of massing and continuity; the reviewer warns that the great becomes turgid and the pathetic insipid in such hands (example: decorating Chimboraco with roseate tints turns the sublime into a 'jeweller's toy').

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of massing and continuity (unity and structural breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no principle of massing or of continuity in his productions — neither height nor breadth nor depth of capacity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works for structural unity, continuity of thought, and capacity to sustain large subjects; lack of 'massing' or continuity is a substantive flaw in a poet aiming at greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of representation and strong internal feeling (authenticity & emotional depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no truth of representation, no strong internal feeling' (critique of superficiality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favour writing that exhibits genuine, inward feeling and truthful representation of experience; avoid lip‑deep sentimentality that lacks emotional reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affected airs, florid superficiality, and sentimental coquetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet shows 'a continual flutter and display of affected airs and graces... All is flimsy, all is florid to excess.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of ornament that masks lack of symmetry or passion; do not substitute extravagant dress for real structural or emotional substance (antipattern: 'converts the wild harp of Erin into a musical snuff‑box').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate imagination and accurate, appropriate similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and fanciful devices should fit the subject (critique: 'This simile is fine, and would have been perfect, but that the moon is not red...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor and analogy must be accurate and relevant; avoid 'enigmatical ingenuity' and fanciful images that contradict fact or undermine the scene (e.g., mock‑heroic fancies in scenes of blood and death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine patriotic feeling in national songs (substance over prettiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Irish Melodies: if these express the soul of impassioned feeling ... otherwise 'if these prettinesses pass for patriotism, the case of Ireland is hopeless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National or patriotic verse should awaken liberty or console humanity — not be mere varnished prettiness or ornamented sentiment; avoid using prettiness as a substitute for political or moral force ('musical snuff‑box').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharpness and economy in political satire and squibs
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's political squibs are 'essences, are
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise, bitter‑sweet squibs that hit off an official manner or fashionable affectation are praiseworthy; effective satire should pierce and expose vanity and folly without diffuse ornament (examples: accurate mimicry of a formalist's set speeches, 'delicate insinuation and adroit satire').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational vivacity and immediate personal charm (effective voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His natural gaiety and sprightliness of manner... produce an immediate fascination and intoxication... in conversation he is all life and animation. A light, familiar grace, and mild unpretending pathos are the characteristics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value a writer whose written voice captures the liveliness and charm of his conversation; such immediacy can redeem stylistic faults, but its effectiveness often depends on the reader's sympathy and perception ('To be admired, he needs but to be seen').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone consonant with the author's persona ('author translates admirably into the man')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The author translates admirably into the man. Indeed the very faults of his style are virtues in the individual.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether stylistic traits reflect a coherent authorial persona; where persona matches prose, idiosyncrasies may be tolerable or even virtuous. Distinguish persona‑based charm from mere excusable lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for antiquarian, obscure, and local subjects (subject selection and point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He prefers bye‑ways to highways... has the very soul of an antiquarian... delights to dwell on that which is fresh to the eye of memory... the shadowy has to our author something substantial in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the value of focusing on the past, local detail, and the obscure; quaintness, moral chiaroscuro, and retrospective tone are legitimate aesthetic choices that produce 'vivid obscurity' and picturesque quaintness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and avoidance of ostentation in style and convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His convictions do not... set off to the world in the glistering foil of fashion... He does not court popularity, nor strut in gaudy plumes, but shrinks from every kind of ostentatious and obvious pretension.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise restraint, modesty, and aversion to fashionable grandstanding; works that eschew sensationalism and grand theories in favour of subtle, honest expression are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and contemporary relevance vs. imitation ('literary anachronisms')
rubrics_metrics.description: On Washington Irving: 'has culled and transplanted the flowers of modern literature... his writings are literary anachronisms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique imitation of earlier models that yields works lacking freshness and probability; writers should observe and render contemporary life rather than transcribe past fashions into the present (antipattern: treating England as if it still were Addison's era).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic economy — dialogue that tends to action and stage‑worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Virginius: 'All his dialogue tends to action, all his situations form classic groups. There is no impertinent display, no flaunting poetry; the writer immediately conceives how a thought would tell if he had to speak it himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama, favour economy and functionality in dialogue (every line should further action); favour playwrights who write with stage performance in mind and avoid decorative but inert verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural feeling, simplicity, and fidelity to truth in dramatic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ignorant alike of rules, regardless of models, he follows the steps of truth and simplicity; and strength, proportion, and delicacy are the infallible results.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value instinctive dramatic genius that relies on simplicity and truth rather than contrived adherence to rules; naturalness yields strength and proportion, producing effective art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated taste and selective reading as a source of depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Lamb's 'taste in books is also fine, and it is peculiar... No one is more unimpressible to a specious declamation; no one relishes a recondite beauty more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a writer's depth by the selectivity and discernment of their reading and critical taste; cultivated eccentricity in taste can enhance the subtlety and authenticity of writing.
